summary: Gives a history and description of the Internet Activities Board and its subsidiary organizations. It is a revision of RFC 1120 and informational only.

plainLanguage.summary: This tells the story of the group that guided the Internet and the smaller teams under it, in an updated edition.

questions: what is the internet activities board

what did the iab do in 1990
subtitle: A 1990 snapshot of the Internet Activities Board, its two task forces, its members and its agenda.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, people needed to know who guided its technical development, how that group was organised and what it was working on.
tldr.mechanism: The memo tells the history from packet switching to the IAB, describes the IAB and its two task forces (the IETF and the IRTF), lists the members, and sets out seven areas of focus for 1989 to 1990.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational snapshot dated May 1990 that revises RFC 1120. It does not define a standard.

today: RFC 1160 is an Informational memo from May 1990 and does not constitute a standard. It revises and replaces RFC 1120, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the IAB and its members as they stood in 1990.

sections.title: From Packet Switching to the IAB
sections.content:
The memo opens in 1968, when DARPA started the effort that became packet switching. Packet radio and packet satellite then raised the question of linking the ARPANET to other kinds of packet networks. Cerf and Kahn proposed an internetwork protocol and gateways, which grew into the TCP/IP protocol suite.

In 1979 the activity had grown enough that an informal committee, the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB), was formed to guide the suite's technical evolution. In January 1983 the Defense Communications Agency declared TCP/IP the standard for the ARPANET, and all systems moved from the earlier Network Control Program. Later that year the ICCB was reorganised around task forces and renamed the Internet Activities Board.

US government funders coordinated through the FRICC, which in 1990 was reorganised into the Federal Networking Council. An international forum, the CCIRN, brought together North American and European research networking bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: A few researchers started sharing computers, then there were too many to coordinate, so a small committee was formed to keep everyone heading the same way.

sections.title: What the IAB Is and Does
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering and management. The memo describes the Internet as over two thousand packet switched networks using the TCP/IP suite. The IAB is an independent committee of researchers and professionals. Its chairman serves a two-year term, is elected by the members, and appoints new members with the advice and consent of the others.

The IAB lists six functions: setting Internet Standards, managing the RFC publication process, reviewing the IETF and IRTF, strategic planning, acting as international technical liaison, and resolving technical issues that the task forces cannot. All IAB decisions are made public, mainly through the RFC series. The IAB meets quarterly, and two of those meetings are normally by video teleconference.

A Standard Protocol starts as a Proposed Standard and may be promoted to Draft Standard and finally Standard after review, implementation and testing. Before a Proposed Standard is published, it is made available as an Internet-Draft, and drafts are either submitted for publication or discarded within 3 to 6 months.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB is like a school council. It decides the big rules, checks on the clubs underneath it and shares what it decided with everyone.

sections.title: The Internet Engineering Task Force
sections.content:
The IETF coordinates the operation, management and evolution of the Internet. It is led by a chairman and managed by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). Its charter covers specifying short and mid-term protocols and architecture and recommending standards for IAB approval, providing an information-exchange forum, and convening Working Groups on pressing problem areas.

It is a large, open community of network designers, operators, vendors and researchers, organised into eight technical areas, each run by an area director. The areas are Applications, Host and User Services, Internet Services, Routing, Network Management, OSI Integration, Operations and Security. The area directors plus the chairman make up the IESG. The memo says there are more than 40 Working Groups. Each has a narrow focus and a lifetime bounded by a specific task, though there are exceptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is the big group of builders who actually work out how things should connect, split into teams by topic.

sections.title: The Internet Research Task Force
sections.content:
The IRTF exists to promote research in networking and the development of new technology. The memo admits the line between research and engineering is blurry, so the IETF and IRTF overlap, including in membership, which it calls vital for cross-fertilization and technology transfer. The IRTF is generally more concerned with understanding than with products or standard protocols.

It is governed by the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG) and organised into Research Groups. Their chairs are appointed by the IRSG chairman, and these groups typically have 10 to 20 members. Each covers a broad research area chosen partly by member interest and partly by IAB recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: If the IETF builds today's bridges, the IRTF is the team asking how bridges work and what better ones might look like.

sections.title: The 1989 to 1990 Agenda
sections.content:
The memo names seven principal foci for 1989 to 1990: Operational Stability, User Services, OSI Coexistence, Testbed Facilities, Security, Getting Big and Getting Fast.

Among the specific points: better tools for gathering operational data and isolating faults, a common internal gateway routing protocol across router vendors, and a major effort toward conformance with the Host Requirements RFCs. For user services, the White Pages mailbox directory is called the most pressing need, and the memo recommends populating directories such as X.500. It also asks for faster deployment of privacy-enhanced electronic mail.

On growth, attention should go to scaling to hundreds of millions of users and hundreds of thousands of networks, and to the limits of the architecture at gigabit speeds. The Internet should also be positioned to support OSI protocols by the end of 1990 or sooner. The memo contains no separate security section, but its security focus calls for guidance and documentation for host managers.
sections.plainLanguage: The council's to-do list: keep things running, make it easy to find people, get ready for much bigger and faster, and stay safe.
